Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Put $S=\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}M^{1/2}$. Multiplying the O equation by the deterministic integrating factor $e^{\gamma t}$ and applying [F3] componentwise gives $d(e^{\gamma t}P_t)=e^{\gamma t}S\,dW_t$. Integrating from $0$ to $h$ and multiplying by $e^{-\gamma h}$ yields [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, algebra]
$$P_h=e^{-\gamma h}P_0+\int_0^h e^{-\gamma(h-s)}S\,dW_s.$$
The integrand is deterministic and square-integrable. By [F2] the integral is centered Gaussian, independent of the starting sigma algebra, with covariance
$$\int_0^h e^{-2\gamma(h-s)}SS^T\,ds=2\gamma\beta^{-1}M\int_0^h e^{-2\gamma(h-s)}ds=\beta^{-1}(1-e^{-2\gamma h})M.$$

By [F4], the displayed covariance has square root $\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-e^{-2\gamma h})}M^{1/2}$. A centered Gaussian vector with this covariance has the same law as that matrix times $\xi\sim N_d(0,I_d)$; [F2] gives independence from the starting sigma algebra. This proves the exact transition and conditional moments.

derivations.claim: The power bound gives $\|A^jGG^T(A^T)^j\|\le C^2\theta^{2j}\|G\|^2$. The geometric series therefore converges entrywise and in matrix norm. Each summand is symmetric positive semidefinite because $x^TA^jGG^T(A^T)^jx=|G^T(A^T)^jx|^2\ge0$, so $P$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Shifting the summation index gives $APA^T+GG^T=P$.

Let $Z\sim N_d(0,P)$ and $\xi\sim N_m(0,I_m)$ be independent; [F3] supplies their finite product probability space. By [F1]–[F2], $AZ+G\xi$ has characteristic function $u\mapsto\exp[-\tfrac12u^T(APA^T+GG^T)u]=\exp[-\tfrac12u^TPu]$. The covariance identity in step 1.1 and [F4] show that $AZ+G\xi$ has the same law as $Z$. Thus $N_d(0,P)$ is invariant.

Let $\nu$ be any invariant probability law and let $\varphi(u)=\int e^{iu\cdot x}\,\nu(dx)$. Invariance and independence of a fresh innovation imply [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
$$\varphi(u)=\varphi(A^Tu)\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12u^TGG^Tu\right).$$
Iterating $n$ times gives
$$\varphi(u)=\varphi((A^T)^nu)\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12u^T\left[\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}A^jGG^T(A^T)^j\right]u\right).$$
The power bound gives $(A^T)^nu\to0$, so the dominated convergence theorem [F5] in the integral defining $\varphi$ gives $\varphi((A^T)^nu)\to1$. Step 1.1 makes the matrix sum converge to $P$, whence $\varphi(u)=e^{-u^TPu/2}$, the characteristic function of the invariant Gaussian from step 2.1. By [F4], $\nu=N_d(0,P)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.

Suppose there are $C<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ such that $\|A^n\|\le C\theta^n$ for every integer $n\ge0$. A probability law $\nu$ is **invariant** for this recursion if, whenever $Z_0\sim\nu$ is independent of a fresh $\xi_1\sim N_m(0,I_m)$, the updated state $AZ_0+G\xi_1$ also has law $\nu$. Consider the Markov chain
$$Z_{n+1}=AZ_n+G\xi_{n+1},$$
where each $\xi_{n+1}\sim N_m(0,I_m)$ is independent of the current state and of the earlier innovations. Then the chain has a unique invariant probability law. It is $N_d(0,P)$, where the convergent positive-semidefinite series
$$P=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}A^jGG^T(A^T)^j$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $H\in M_d(\mathbb R)$,
the square-matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]],
be symmetric positive definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]. Let $\lambda_d$ denote
the Lebesgue measure of
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Interpret the
displayed integral as the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\exp\!\left(-\frac12 u^{\mathsf T}Hu\right)\,d\lambda_d(u) =\frac{(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\sqrt{\det H}}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

1. **B half kick:** $p^{(1)}=p_n-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_n)$.
2. **A half drift:** $q^{(1)}=q_n+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(1)}$.
3. **O full thermostat:** $p^{(2)}=a p^{(1)}+\sqrt{\beta^{-1}(1-a^2)}M^{1/2}\xi_n$.
4. **A half drift:** $q_{n+1}=q^{(1)}+\tfrac h2M^{-1}p^{(2)}$.
5. **B half kick:** $p_{n+1}=p^{(2)}-\tfrac h2\nabla V(q_{n+1})$.

The output is $(q_{n+1},p_{n+1})$. If any required gradient is undefined or any input violates $h>0$, $\beta>0$, $\gamma>0$, or positive definiteness of $M$, return `failure` without an updated state. For a differentiable $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ and finite valid state, both gradient calls are defined; reusing the stored value $\nabla V(q_{n+1})$ as the next step's first force means one new force evaluation per subsequent step. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

Differentiating these explicit maps and taking Gaussian expectations therefore shows that each $P_s^C$, $C\in\{A,B,O\}$, preserves bounds $|D^j\psi(z)|\le K_0W_r(z)$ through any stated order $k\le6$, uniformly for $s\le1$. Each generator maps such bounds through order $k$ to bounds through order $k-2$ with weight $W_{r+1}$: its drift coefficients grow at most linearly, their positive-order derivatives are bounded, and its second-order coefficients are constant. Thus a composition with at most three generator applications, even with subflow semigroups between them, uses at most six test derivatives and is bounded by $CW_{p+3}(z)$.

For any $r\ge0$, direct differentiation of $W_r$ and the linear-growth drift and constant diffusion give $|LW_r|\le C_rW_r$. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be finite, let $M\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be symmetric positive definite (that is, $x^TMx>0$ for every nonzero $x$), and let $\beta,\gamma>0$. Then $M$ is invertible, and $M^{1/2}$ denotes its unique symmetric positive square root. Let $W_t$ be standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to a complete usual filtration, and let $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. The **underdamped Langevin equation** is the It\^o SDE on phase space $\mathbb R^d_q\times\mathbb R^d_p$
$$dQ_t=M^{-1}P_t\,dt,\qquad dP_t=-\nabla V(Q_t)\,dt-\gamma P_t\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma\beta^{-1}}\,M^{1/2}dW_t.$$
Its Hamiltonian is $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$. If $Z=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}\,dq\,dp$ is finite and positive, the **canonical Gibbs probability** is the probability measure with density $\rho(q,p)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(q,p)}$ with respect to $2d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. This definition alone asserts no stationarity or ergodicity.

For the finite-time order results below, $D^jV$ denotes the $j$th derivative as a multilinear map. The notation $C_b^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded. The notation $C_P^k$ means that a function and each of its derivatives through order $k$ are continuous and bounded by $C(1+|z|^r)$ for some finite constants $C,r$ that may depend on the derivative. These growth conventions are used only where stated.

Let $d=1$, $M=m>0$, $V(q)=kq^2/2$ with $k>0$, and $\beta,\gamma,h>0$. Put
$$\omega^2=\frac{k}{m},\qquad r=\frac{h^2\omega^2}{4}=\frac{h^2k}{4m},\qquad a=e^{-\gamma h}.$$
For $0<h<2\sqrt{m/k}$, the BAOAB chain of [[alg-baoab-underdamped-langevin-splitting]] has the unique invariant law
$$\begin{pmatrix}Q\\P\end{pmatrix}\sim N_2\!\left(0,\begin{pmatrix}(\beta k)^{-1}&0\\0&(m/\beta)(1-r)\end{pmatrix}\right).$$
Thus the position variance is exactly the canonical Gibbs variance $1/(\beta k)$, while the momentum variance has bias $-h^2k/(4\beta)$ relative to the canonical value $m/\beta$. The linear transition matrix $A$ in proof step 1.2 has spectral radius $\rho(A):=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\text{ is a complex eigenvalue of }A\}$ less than one exactly for $0<h<2\sqrt{m/k}$; at equality its spectral radius is one, and for $h>2\sqrt{m/k}$ the chain has no invariant probability law. No conclusion about nonquadratic potentials or general BAOAB superconvergence follows from this harmonic calculation.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
